title: Why Earth's First Animals Were Stuck in Slow-Mo for Millions of Years
summary:
Have you ever seen a strawberry plant send out runners to make new plants? That's exactly how some of Earth's first animals made babies — for millions of years! And it turns out, that was a big reason why life stayed kind of boring for so long.

A new study from the University of Cambridge looked at weird, fern-like creatures called Fractofusus that lived over 500 million years ago. These animals didn't have mouths or guts. They just soaked up food from the water. And when they reproduced, they grew long runners (like strawberry plants) that sprouted identical copies of themselves.

"Life was pretty nice during the Ediacaran, so the need for sex was rather limited," said Dr. Emily Mitchell, who led the study. Because these clones were all connected, they shared nutrients and didn't have to compete. That sounds friendly, but it meant evolution was stuck in slow motion. No competition, no big changes.

The scientists used lasers and artificial intelligence to study fossils from Newfoundland, Canada. They even ran thousands of computer simulations to see how these ancient communities worked. The results showed that when animals finally started spreading out and having sex, diversity exploded. Stressful environments — like storms and changing temperatures — may have pushed them to try something new.

So, the next time you see a strawberry patch, remember: those runners once ruled the world, until sex changed everything!
why_it_matters: Just like in a classroom or sports team, a little bit of challenge and mixing with different people helps you grow and get better — life works the same way.

background_read: The University of Cambridge (a famous university in England) led this study of ancient life.
These creatures lived during the Ediacaran period (a time long before dinosaurs, about 635–541 million years ago), when all life was in the ocean.
Fractofusus were among the first complex multicellular organisms on Earth, but they had no mouths, brains, or legs — they simply absorbed food from the water around them.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists from the University of Cambridge, led by Dr. Emily Mitchell.
WHAT: They discovered that early animals like Fractofusus reproduced by cloning with runners, which slowed evolution for millions of years.
WHERE: Fossils were studied from Newfoundland, Canada, and computer simulations ran in a lab.
WHY: To understand why life stayed simple for so long and what finally triggered big changes.

perspectives.description: Cloning and sharing nutrients meant early animals lived in peaceful, connected colonies without fighting over food.
Without competition and sexual reproduction, evolution slowed down, and life stayed boring and unchanging for millions of years.
Harsh environments like storms and temperature shifts may have finally pushed animals to try sexual reproduction, sparking the explosion of diversity we see today.
